        <label>Tokens per word  d  =  <span class="val" id="dv">1.50</span>
           —  <span class="flash">a free label: move it and nothing changes</span>
        </label>
        <input type="range" id="d" min="1.00" max="2.20" step="0.01" value="1.50">
      </div>

      <div>
        <div style="color:var(--dim);font-size:.8rem;text-transform:uppercase;
                    letter-spacing:.06em">keys you must keep</div>
        <div class="big" id="knee">14</div>
        <table>
          <tr><th>quantity</th><th class="num">value</th></tr>
          <tr><td>top‑key mass  p₀</td><td class="num" id="p0"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>collision index  S = Σ p<sub>i</sub>²</td>
              <td class="num" id="S"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>effective #keys  1/S</td><td class="num" id="eff"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>top‑mass bound  τ/p₀</td>
              <td class="num" id="b1"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>participation bound  τ²/S</td>
              <td class="num" id="b2"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>residual at the knee  r<sup>k*</sup></td>
              <td class="num" id="res"></td></tr>
        </table>
        <p class="note" id="verdict"></p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="cv" width="1060" height="380"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      <b>Bars</b>: the attention mass held by each key, sorted heaviest first.
      <b>Blue curve</b>: the capture curve C(k), the mass held by the k heaviest
      keys. The dashed line is the tolerance τ; the knee k* is the first
      integer where the curve reaches it. The two vertical markers are the
      certified lower bounds τ/p₀ and τ²/S — they can never
      lie to the right of the knee.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h3 style="margin:0 0 4px;font-size:1.05rem">The knee curve — the whole invariant</h3>
    <canvas id="cv2" width="1060" height="260"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      The knee is not one number but a curve τ ↦ k*(τ). Two domains
      with the same knee curve have the <i>same</i> attention concentration, so
      this curve is a complete fingerprint of a domain's memory behaviour. The
      grey curves are the other presets: notice they never cross — a
      uniformly more concentrated domain is uniformly cheaper, at every
      tolerance. That is the duality between knee dominance and majorization.
    </p>

    <details>
      <summary>Why can the bounds never overtake the knee? (click to reveal the proofs)</summary>
      <p style="font-size:.93rem">
        <b>Top‑mass bound.</b> Since the mass vector is sorted, every key holds
        at most p₀. So the k heaviest keys hold at most k·p₀. At
        the knee this must reach τ, giving k* ≥ τ/p₀.
      </p>
      <p style="font-size:.93rem">
        <b>Participation bound.</b> By Cauchy–Schwarz,
        C(k)² = (Σ<sub>i<k</sub> p<sub>i</sub>·1)²
        ≤ k · Σ<sub>i<k</sub> p<sub>i</sub>² ≤ k·S.
        Putting k = k* and C(k*) ≥ τ gives k* ≥ τ²/S. The
        quantity 1/S is the classical <i>effective number of participating
        keys</i>; the bound says a domain that genuinely spreads its attention
        over many keys cannot be compressed below that number, up to the factor
        τ².
      </p>
      <p style="font-size:.93rem">
        <b>Exact solution for this family.</b> With C(k) = 1 − r<sup>k</sup>,
        keeping k keys suffices exactly when the leftover mass r<sup>k</sup> has
        fallen below the slack 1 − τ. So
        k*(τ) = ⌈ log(1−τ) / log r ⌉.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const rEl = $('r'), tEl = $('t'), dEl = $('d');
  const cv = $('cv'), ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
  const cv2 = $('cv2'), ctx2 = cv2.getContext('2d');
  const PRESETS = [0.90, 0.70, 0.55, 0.50];

  function kneeOf(r, tau){
    let k = 0, residual = 1, slack = 1 - tau;
    while (residual > slack + 1e-15 && k < 5000){ residual *= r; k++; }
    return k;
  }
  function stats(r){
    // p_i = (1-r) r^i  -> p0 = 1-r, S = (1-r)^2/(1-r^2) = (1-r)/(1+r)
    const p0 = 1 - r;
    const S  = (1 - r) / (1 + r);
    return {p0:p0, S:S};
  }

  function drawMain(){
    const r = +rEl.value, tau = +tEl.value, d = +dEl.value;
    $('rv').textContent = r.toFixed(2);
    $('tv').textContent = tau.toFixed(2);
    $('dv').textContent = d.toFixed(2);

    const k = kneeOf(r, tau);
    const {p0, S} = stats(r);
    const b1 = tau / p0, b2 = tau*tau / S;
    $('knee').textContent = k;
    $('p0').textContent  = p0.toFixed(4);
    $('S').textContent   = S.toFixed(4);
    $('eff').textContent = (1/S).toFixed(2);
    $('b1').textContent  = b1.toFixed(2);
    $('b2').textContent  = b2.toFixed(2);
    $('res').textContent = Math.pow(r, k).toFixed(4);
    $('verdict').innerHTML =
      'Both certified bounds hold: ' +
      '<b>' + Math.max(b1,b2).toFixed(2) + ' ≤ k* = ' + k + '</b>. ' +
      'Tokens per word is ' + d.toFixed(2) + ' — and it appears nowhere ' +
      'in the computation of the knee.';

    // ---- canvas 1 ----
    const W = cv.width, H = cv.height, L = 62, R = 24, T = 22, B = 44;
    const N = 40;
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    const x = i => L + (W-L-R) * i / N;
    const yC = v => H - B - (H-T-B) * v;

    // grid
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#26304a'; ctx.lineWidth = 1; ctx.font = '12px sans-serif';
    ctx.fillStyle = '#96a2b8';
    for (let g=0; g<=5; g++){
      const v = g/5, yy = yC(v);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L, yy); ctx.lineTo(W-R, yy); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillText(v.toFixed(1), 24, yy+4);
    }
    for (let i=0; i<=N; i+=5){
      ctx.fillText(i, x(i)-6, H-B+18);
    }
    ctx.fillText('key index k', W/2-34, H-8);

    // mass bars (scaled to the largest so they are visible)
    const masses = [];
    for (let i=0;i<N;i++) masses.push((1-r)*Math.pow(r,i));
    const mmax = masses[0];
    const bw = (W-L-R)/N * 0.62;
    for (let i=0;i<N;i++){
      const h = (H-T-B) * (masses[i]/mmax) * 0.42;
      ctx.fillStyle = (i < k) ? 'rgba(92,230,161,0.55)' : 'rgba(150,162,184,0.22)';
      ctx.fillRect(x(i)+2, H-B-h, bw, h);
    }

    // capture curve
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#5cc8ff'; ctx.lineWidth = 2.4; ctx.beginPath();
    for (let i=0;i<=N;i++){
      const v = 1 - Math.pow(r,i);
      if (i===0) ctx.moveTo(x(i), yC(v)); else ctx.lineTo(x(i), yC(v));
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    // tolerance line
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#ffb454'; ctx.setLineDash([7,5]); ctx.lineWidth = 1.8;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L, yC(tau)); ctx.lineTo(W-R, yC(tau)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle = '#ffb454';
    ctx.fillText('tolerance \u03C4 = ' + tau.toFixed(2), W-R-140, yC(tau)-8);

    // knee marker
    if (k <= N){
      ctx.strokeStyle = '#5ce6a1'; ctx.lineWidth = 2;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x(k), H-B); ctx.lineTo(x(k), yC(1-Math.pow(r,k))); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillStyle = '#5ce6a1';
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x(k), yC(1-Math.pow(r,k)), 5, 0, 7); ctx.fill();
      ctx.font = 'bold 13px sans-serif';
      ctx.fillText('k* = ' + k, x(k)+8, yC(1-Math.pow(r,k))-10);
      ctx.font = '12px sans-serif';
    } else {
      ctx.fillStyle = '#ff6b81'; ctx.font = 'bold 13px sans-serif';
      ctx.fillText('k* = ' + k + '  (beyond this window \u2014 a censored measurement!)',
                   L+16, T+18);
      ctx.font = '12px sans-serif';
    }

    // bound markers
    const mark = (v, col, lab) => {
      if (v > N) return;
      ctx.strokeStyle = col; ctx.setLineDash([3,4]); ctx.lineWidth = 1.6;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x(v), H-B); ctx.lineTo(x(v), T+30); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.setLineDash([]); ctx.fillStyle = col;
      ctx.fillText(lab, x(v)+4, T+26);
    };
    mark(b1, '#c792ea', '\u03C4/p\u2080');
    mark(b2, '#ff6b81', '\u03C4\u00B2/S');

    drawKneeCurve(r, tau);
  }

  function drawKneeCurve(rNow, tauNow){
    const W = cv2.width, H = cv2.height, L = 62, R = 24, T = 18, B = 40;
    ctx2.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    const KMAX = 40;
    const x = t => L + (W-L-R) * (t - 0.02) / 0.96;
    const y = k => H - B - (H-T-B) * Math.min(k, KMAX) / KMAX;

    ctx2.strokeStyle = '#26304a'; ctx2.lineWidth = 1;
    ctx2.font = '12px sans-serif'; ctx2.fillStyle = '#96a2b8';
    for (let g=0; g<=4; g++){
      const kk = g*KMAX/4, yy = y(kk);
      ctx2.beginPath(); ctx2.moveTo(L,yy); ctx2.lineTo(W-R,yy); ctx2.stroke();
      ctx2.fillText(kk.toFixed(0), 30, yy+4);
    }
    for (let g=0; g<=4; g++){
      const tt = 0.02 + 0.96*g/4;
      ctx2.fillText(tt.toFixed(2), x(tt)-12, H-B+18);
    }
    ctx2.fillText('tolerance \u03C4', W/2-34, H-6);
    ctx2.save(); ctx2.translate(16, H/2+30); ctx2.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
    ctx2.fillText('knee k*(\u03C4)', 0, 0); ctx2.restore();

    const plot = (r, col, lw) => {
      ctx2.strokeStyle = col; ctx2.lineWidth = lw; ctx2.beginPath();
      let first = true;
      for (let t = 0.02; t <= 0.98; t += 0.01){
        const k = kneeOf(r, t);
        if (first){ ctx2.moveTo(x(t), y(k)); first = false; }
        else ctx2.lineTo(x(t), y(k));
      }
      ctx2.stroke();
    };
    PRESETS.forEach(p => plot(p, 'rgba(150,162,184,0.35)', 1.6));
    plot(rNow, '#5cc8ff', 2.8);

    const kk = kneeOf(rNow, tauNow);
    ctx2.fillStyle = '#5ce6a1';
    ctx2.beginPath(); ctx2.arc(x(tauNow), y(kk), 5, 0, 7); ctx2.fill();
  }

  [rEl,tEl,dEl].forEach(el => el.addEventListener('input', drawMain));
  document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach(c => {
    c.addEventListener('click', () => {
      document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach(o => o.classList.remove('on'));
      c.classList.add('on');
      rEl.value = c.dataset.preset;
      drawMain();
    });
  });
  drawMain();
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "The Refutation Explorer: Can Any Law of Token Density Fit?",
      "description": "A hands-on refutation sandbox. The four measured domains are fixed at their true tokens-per-word values, but their knees are yours to move. As you drag them the panel recomputes, live, the Spearman coefficient, the coefficient of determination, both rank vectors, and — the decisive test — an explicit search for a discordant pair and a concordant pair. Whenever a discordant pair exists the explorer names it and declares every strictly increasing law refuted, with the reason spelled out in the domains' own numbers; likewise a concordant pair refutes every strictly decreasing law. The scatter panel draws the least-squares line and highlights both certificate pairs as coloured arrows, with the censored French point marked for reference. Preset buttons restore the measured data, jump to a genuinely monotone configuration where the certificates vanish and the correlation reaches one, and to a flat configuration with no variance at all. The lesson the widget teaches is that it is not the shape of the fit that fails on the real data — it is the order.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>The Refutation Explorer — can any law of token density fit?</title>
<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0e1117; --panel:#161b26; --ink:#e8edf6; --dim:#96a2b8;
    --accent:#5cc8ff; --good:#5ce6a1; --warn:#ffb454; --bad:#ff6b81;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
       font-family:ui-sans-serif,-apple-system,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;
       line-height:1.55}
  .wrap{max-width:1120px;margin:0 auto;padding:26px 20px 60px}
  h1{font-size:1.55rem;margin:0 0 4px}
  .sub{color:var(--dim);margin:0 0 22px}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid #232c40;border-radius:14px;
         padding:18px 20px;margin-bottom:18px}
  .grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1.15fr 1fr;gap:20px}
  @media(max-width:900px){.grid{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  canvas{width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:10px;background:#0b0f18}
  label{display:block;font-size:.84rem;color:var(--dim);margin:12px 0 3px;
        text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.05em}
  input[type=range]{width:100%;accent-color:var(--accent)}
  .val{color:var(--accent);font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;font-weight:600}
  .stat{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;
        padding:9px 0;border-bottom:1px solid #232c40}
  .stat b{font-size:1.5rem;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  .ok{color:var(--good)} .no{color:var(--bad)} .mid{color:var(--warn)}
  .verdict{margin-top:14px;padding:12px 14px;border-radius:10px;font-size:.95rem;
           background:#0b0f18;border-left:4px solid var(--bad)}
  .verdict.pass{border-left-color:var(--good)}
  button{background:#1e2740;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid #2b3550;
         border-radius:9px;padding:7px 14px;cursor:pointer;margin:8px 8px 0 0;
         font-size:.88rem}
  button:hover{border-color:var(--accent)}
  .note{font-size:.9rem;color:var(--dim)}
  details{margin-top:12px;border-left:3px solid #2b3550;padding-left:14px}
  summary{cursor:pointer;color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;font-size:.94rem}
  code{background:#0b0f18;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;color:var(--accent)}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Refutation Explorer</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Four domains, each with a fixed tokens‑per‑word and an adjustable
    knee. Try to move the knees so that some increasing law of token density
    could explain them — the explorer tells you instantly, with a
    certificate, when you have failed.
  </p>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="grid">
      <div>
        <canvas id="cv" width="640" height="430"></canvas>
        <div>
          <button id="reset">Reset to the measured data</button>
          <button id="make">Make it monotone</button>
          <button id="flat">Make it flat</button>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div>
        <div id="sliders"></div>
        <div class="stat"><span>Spearman ρ</span><b id="rho"></b></div>
        <div class="stat"><span>Coefficient of determination R²</span>
             <b id="r2"></b></div>
        <div class="stat"><span>rank vector by density</span>
             <b id="rk1" style="font-size:1.05rem"></b></div>
        <div class="stat"><span>rank vector by knee</span>
             <b id="rk2" style="font-size:1.05rem"></b></div>
        <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <p class="note">
      <b>What you are testing.</b> Pre‑registered prediction P1 asked for a
      rank correlation ρ ≥ 0.9 between token density and the knee; P2 asked
      for R² ≥ 0.8. On the measured data the answers are ρ = −0.40
      and R² ≈ 0.004. But the decisive test is not either number: it is
      whether a single <i>discordant pair</i> exists.
    </p>
    <details open>
      <summary>The No‑Monotone‑Law Principle (click to expand)</summary>
      <p style="font-size:.94rem">
        Suppose two observables x and y are measured on the same items. If there
        are items i, j with <code>xᵢ < xⱼ</code> but
        <code>yⱼ ≤ yᵢ</code> — a <b>discordant pair</b> — then
        there is <b>no</b> strictly increasing function f at all with y = f(x).
        The proof is one line: f preserves strict order, so
        xᵢ < xⱼ would force yᵢ < yⱼ.
      </p>
      <p style="font-size:.94rem">
        Dually, a <b>concordant pair</b> (<code>xᵢ < xⱼ</code> and
        <code>yᵢ < yⱼ</code>) rules out every strictly decreasing law.
        The measured data has both, so neither direction survives — and
        neither does any nonlinear reparameterisation, because monotone maps
        cannot create or destroy discordance.
      </p>
      <p style="font-size:.94rem">
        This is why one cannot rescue the hypothesis by fitting a curve instead
        of a line: it is not the shape of the fit that fails, it is the order.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const NAMES = ['code','prose-de','math','prose-en'];
  const TPW   = [1.950, 1.885, 1.214, 1.173];
  const BASE  = [12, 20, 16, 16];
  let knees = BASE.slice();

  const box = $('sliders');
  NAMES.forEach((n,i) => {
    const lab = document.createElement('label');
    lab.innerHTML = n + '  —  TPW ' + TPW[i].toFixed(3) +
                    '    knee = <span class="val" id="kv'+i+'">' +
                    knees[i] + '</span>';
    const s = document.createElement('input');
    s.type='range'; s.min=1; s.max=40; s.step=1; s.value=knees[i]; s.id='k'+i;
    s.addEventListener('input', () => { knees[i] = +s.value; render(); });
    box.appendChild(lab); box.appendChild(s);
  });

  function ordinalRanks(v){
    const idx = v.map((x,i)=>i).sort((a,b)=> v[a]-v[b] || a-b);
    const r = new Array(v.length);
    idx.forEach((i,p)=> r[i]=p+1);
    return r;
  }
  function spearman(a,b){
    const n=a.length; let s=0;
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++) s += (a[i]-b[i])*(a[i]-b[i]);
    return 1 - 6*s/(n*(n*n-1));
  }
  function rsq(x,y){
    const n=x.length;
    const mx=x.reduce((p,c)=>p+c,0)/n, my=y.reduce((p,c)=>p+c,0)/n;
    let sxy=0,sxx=0,syy=0;
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ sxy+=(x[i]-mx)*(y[i]-my); sxx+=(x[i]-mx)**2; syy+=(y[i]-my)**2; }
    if (syy === 0 || sxx === 0) return 0;
    return sxy*sxy/(sxx*syy);
  }
  function findPair(x,y,kind){
    for(let a=0;a<x.length;a++) for(let b=0;b<x.length;b++){
      if (a===b) continue;
      if (x[a]<x[b]){
        if (kind==='disc' && !(y[a]<y[b])) return [a,b];
        if (kind==='conc' &&  (y[a]<y[b])) return [a,b];
      }
    }
    return null;
  }

  function render(){
    NAMES.forEach((n,i)=> $('kv'+i).textContent = knees[i]);
    const rT = ordinalRanks(TPW), rK = ordinalRanks(knees);
    const rho = spearman(rT, rK), R2 = rsq(TPW, knees);
    $('rho').textContent = (rho>=0?'+':'') + rho.toFixed(3);
    $('rho').className = rho >= 0.9 ? 'ok' : (rho < 0 ? 'no' : 'mid');
    const flat = knees.every(k => k === knees[0]);
    $('r2').textContent = flat ? 'undefined (no variance)' : R2.toFixed(4);
    $('r2').className = R2 >= 0.8 ? 'ok' : (R2 < 0.1 ? 'no' : 'mid');
    $('rk1').textContent = '[' + rT.join(', ') + ']';
    $('rk2').textContent = '[' + rK.join(', ') + ']';

    const disc = findPair(TPW, knees, 'disc');
    const conc = findPair(TPW, knees, 'conc');
    const v = $('verdict');
    let html = '';
    if (disc){
      const [a,b] = disc;
      html += '<b class="no">Increasing laws: refuted.</b> Certificate: ' +
        NAMES[a] + ' (TPW ' + TPW[a].toFixed(3) + ', knee ' + knees[a] + ') vs ' +
        NAMES[b] + ' (TPW ' + TPW[b].toFixed(3) + ', knee ' + knees[b] +
        ') — density rises, the knee does not.<br>';
      v.classList.remove('pass');
    } else {
      html += '<b class="ok">No discordant pair: this test does not refute ' +
              'increasing laws \u2014 the ranks are compatible.</b><br>';
      v.classList.add('pass');
    }
    if (conc){
      const [a,b] = conc;
      html += '<b class="no">Decreasing laws: refuted.</b> Certificate: ' +
        NAMES[a] + ' vs ' + NAMES[b] + ' — density and knee rise together.';
    } else {
      html += '<b class="mid">No concordant pair: this test does not refute ' +
              'decreasing laws.</b>';
    }
    v.innerHTML = html;
    draw(disc, conc);
  }

  function draw(disc, conc){
    const cv = $('cv'), ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    const W=cv.width, H=cv.height, L=58, R=22, T=22, B=46;
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    const xmin=1.10, xmax=2.05, ymax=42;
    const X = t => L + (W-L-R)*(t-xmin)/(xmax-xmin);
    const Y = k => H-B - (H-T-B)*k/ymax;

    ctx.strokeStyle='#26304a'; ctx.lineWidth=1; ctx.font='12px sans-serif';
    ctx.fillStyle='#96a2b8';
    for(let g=0; g<=6; g++){
      const k=g*ymax/6, yy=Y(k);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,yy); ctx.lineTo(W-R,yy); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillText(k.toFixed(0), 28, yy+4);
    }
    for(let g=0; g<=4; g++){
      const t=xmin+(xmax-xmin)*g/4;
      ctx.fillText(t.toFixed(2), X(t)-14, H-B+18);
    }
    ctx.fillText('tokens per word', W/2-46, H-10);
    ctx.save(); ctx.translate(16,H/2+22); ctx.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
    ctx.fillText('knee k*',0,0); ctx.restore();

    // least squares line
    const n=4;
    const mx=TPW.reduce((p,c)=>p+c,0)/n, my=knees.reduce((p,c)=>p+c,0)/n;

  "interactive_layout": "# How much of the past does a machine need to remember?

*A guided tour of the memory knee, why token counting fails to predict it, and
what actually does.*

---

## 1. The question, in one picture

When a language model reads, every new token looks back over everything before
it and spreads a fixed budget of *attention* across those earlier positions.
Almost all of that attention lands on a few positions. So a natural engineering
move is to keep only the $k$ heaviest keys and throw the rest away.

How small can $k$ be? The answer is a number called the **knee**, written
$k^*$: the smallest retention budget at which quality stops degrading.

Here is the puzzle. Fix one model, one tokenizer, one context length, and vary
only the *kind of text*:

| domain | tokens per word | knee $k^*$ |
|---|---|---|
| code | $1.950$ | $12$ |
| German prose | $1.885$ | $20$ |
| French prose | $1.246$ | $>32$ |
| mathematics | $1.214$ | $16$ |
| English prose | $1.173$ | $16$ |

Same model, five different memory requirements. Why?

---

## 2. The obvious guess, and why it dies

Models read **tokens**, not words. Code and German fragment into many subword
pieces; English mostly does not. So: *domains whose words cost more tokens
should need more keys.* That is the tokenization-density hypothesis, and two
predictions were stated in advance — a rank correlation of at least $0.9$, and
a straight-line fit explaining at least $80\%$ of the variance.

Look at the top and bottom rows of the table. Code has $1.66$ times English's
token density and needs **fewer** keys. French has essentially English's
density and needs at least **twice** as many.

{{visualization:0}}

The measured rank correlation is $\rho = -2/5 = -0.40$ — negative — and the
linear fit explains $4225/1054258 \approx 0.4\%$ of the variance.

But a correlation is only a summary. Play with the data yourself: move each
domain's knee and watch what it would take for *some* increasing law of token
density to survive.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>The one-line theorem behind the red verdicts</b></summary>

**No-Monotone-Law Principle.** Let $x$ and $y$ be observables on the same
items. If there exist $i, j$ with $x_i < x_j$ but $y_j \le y_i$ — a
**discordant pair** — then there is *no* strictly increasing $f$ with
$y = f(x)$.

*Proof.* A strictly increasing $f$ satisfies $x_i < x_j \Rightarrow f(x_i) <
f(x_j)$, i.e. $y_i < y_j$, contradicting discordance. $\blacksquare$

Dually, a **concordant pair** ($x_i < x_j$ and $y_i < y_j$) rules out every
strictly decreasing law. The measured data contains both, so neither direction
survives — and no nonlinear reparameterisation helps, because monotone maps
cannot create or destroy discordance. That is much stronger than "the
correlation is low".

</details>

The same idea has a rank-level face worth knowing. Assign each domain its
**competition rank** — one plus the number of domains scoring strictly below
it. Competition ranks are unchanged by *any* strictly increasing
reparameterisation, so if a monotone law existed, the two rank vectors would
have to be identical. They are not: code is rank $4$ in density and rank $1$ in
knee.

{{algorithm:1}}

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 3. Modelling a domain by the shape of its attention

Refutation is only half a result. Here is the replacement.

Sort a domain's attention mass so the heaviest key comes first, and define the
**capture curve**
$$C(k) = \text{fraction of attention mass held by the } k \text{ heaviest keys}.$$
It starts at $C(0) = 0$, never decreases, and never exceeds $1$. The knee at
tolerance $\tau \in (0,1)$ is then simply
$$k^*(\tau) = \min\{k : C(k) \ge \tau\}.$$

That is the whole model. Three things follow immediately: the knee grows with
$\tau$; the knee *shrinks* when the capture curve rises; and the knee depends on
the capture curve **and nothing else** — the tokenizer never enters.

Build a domain and see for yourself. Move the decay slider and the knee moves.
Move the tokens-per-word slider and nothing happens at all.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why token density can never predict the knee — the Decoupling Theorem</b></summary>

**Decoupling Theorem.** Fix any tolerance $\tau \in (0,1)$. For every token
density $d$ and every target knee $k \ge 1$ there is a domain with
tokens-per-word exactly $d$ and knee exactly $k$.

*Proof.* Let the top $k$ keys each carry mass $\tau/k$, so
$C(j) = \min(1, j\tau/k)$. Then $C(k) = \tau$ and $C(j) < \tau$ for $j < k$, so
the knee is exactly $k$; attach any density $d$ you like as a label.
$\blacksquare$

**Corollary.** There is no function $g$ *of any kind* with
$k^* = g(\mathrm{TPW})$: a single density supports domains with every possible
knee. So $\rho = -0.40$ and $R^2 = 0.004$ were not bad luck — the map being
fitted does not exist.

</details>

---

## 4. What *does* control the knee

Two bounds, from opposite ends of the attention distribution, pin the knee down.

**Top-mass bound.** If the heaviest key carries mass $p_0$, then
$k^*(\tau) \ge \tau / p_0$.

**Participation bound.** Let $S = \sum_i p_i^2$ be the **collision index** — the
probability that two independent draws from the attention distribution hit the
same key. Its reciprocal $1/S$ is the classical *effective number of
participating keys*. Then
$$k^*(\tau) \;\ge\; \frac{\tau^2}{S}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Both proofs, in three lines each</b></summary>

*Top-mass.* Sortedness gives $p_i \le p_0$, hence $C(k) \le k p_0$. At the knee
$C(k^*) \ge \tau$, so $k^* p_0 \ge \tau$.

*Participation.* Cauchy–Schwarz on the top-$k$ block:
$C(k)^2 = \big(\sum_{i<k} p_i \cdot 1\big)^2 \le k \sum_{i<k} p_i^2 \le kS$.
Put $k = k^*$ and use $C(k^*) \ge \tau$ to get $\tau^2 \le k^* S$.
$\blacksquare$

Notice what is *absent* from both proofs: any mention of tokens. These are
relational statistics of the attention pattern itself.

</details>

Both bounds are computable from a handful of forward passes, and they are hard
floors: provisioning a cache below them is guaranteed to discard mass.

{{algorithm:3}}

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 5. An exactly solvable domain, and the shift reproduced

Take the **geometric domain** with decay rate $r \in (0,1)$, where
$C(k) = 1 - r^k$: the attention left beyond position $k$ decays like $r^k$. Then

$$k^*(\tau) \le k \iff r^k \le 1 - \tau,$$

that is, you may stop as soon as the leftover mass falls under the slack
$1-\tau$. Equivalently $k^*(\tau) = \lceil \log(1-\tau)/\log r\rceil$.

Now fix $\tau = 3/4$ and compare two decay rates:

- $r = 1/2$ needs $2^{-k} \le 1/4$, so $k^* = 2$;
- $r = 9/10$ needs $0.9^k \le 1/4$, so $k^* = 14$.

**A sevenfold gap in memory requirement between two domains with identical token
densities.** That is the code-versus-French gap, in miniature, generated purely
by how fast attention decays.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 6. How much does the knee curve remember?

The knee is really a *curve*: one value $k^*(\tau)$ for each tolerance. How much
of a domain does it know?

Say $P$ **knee-dominates** $Q$ if $P$ needs no more keys at every tolerance, and
say $P$'s attention **majorizes** $Q$'s if $P$'s capture curve is pointwise at
least $Q$'s. Majorization is the classical order behind
[Schur convexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur-convex_function) and the
[Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majorization) of
"more spread out".

> **Duality Theorem.** $P$ knee-dominates $Q$ **if and only if** $P$'s capture
> curve majorizes $Q$'s.

<details>
<summary><b>The hard direction, and the tolerance that does the work</b></summary>

Suppose $C_P(k) < C_Q(k)$ for some $k$. Put a tolerance strictly in the gap,
$$\tau = \tfrac12\big(C_P(k) + C_Q(k)\big) \in (0,1).$$
Then $Q$ reaches $\tau$ by index $k$, so $k^*_Q(\tau) \le k$. But
$C_P(j) \le C_P(k) < \tau$ for every $j \le k$, so $k^*_P(\tau) > k$. Dominance
fails at exactly that tolerance. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary (complete invariance).** If two domains have the same knee at every
tolerance, they have the same capture curve. The knee curve is a faithful
shadow of concentration — but it says nothing whatsoever about the tokenizer.

</details>

And a reassurance about mixed corpora:

> **Mixture Sandwich.** A corpus mixing two domains with weights $\lambda$ and
> $1-\lambda$ has, at every tolerance,
> $\min(k_P^*, k_Q^*) \le k_{\text{mix}}^* \le \max(k_P^*, k_Q^*)$.

So blending can never create a corpus harder than both ingredients or easier
than both — the observed spread across domains is real structure, not an
artifact of how the samples were assembled.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 7. Everything at once

The full numerical tour: the two refuting statistics in exact rational
arithmetic, the certificate pairs, the three concentration bounds checked
against true knees, the decoupling construction, the geometric family, and the
mixture sandwich.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 8. What to take away

1. **Token density is not merely a weak predictor of the memory knee; it is not
   a predictor at all.** Every (density, knee) pair is realisable, so the
   function being fitted does not exist.
2. **The knee is a concentration functional.** It is bounded below by
   $\tau/p_0$ and by $\tau^2/S$, and on geometric decay profiles it is
   determined exactly by the decay rate.
3. **As an order, the knee curve *is* majorization** — a complete invariant of
   the capture curve, stable under mixing.

The practical consequence: budget your key cache by measuring attention
concentration, not by counting tokens. And the conceptual one: the domain shift
is not visible from outside the model. It lives in how far back a given kind of
text forces the model to reach.

# NET-73, cycle 2: the concentration spectrum of a domain

import Mathlib
import Applications.NET73KneeDecoupling

namespace Catalog.NET73

open Finset AttentionProfile

/-! ## 1. Domains presented by a sorted attention mass vector -/

/-- A domain presented by its attention mass vector, sorted in nonincreasing
order and supported on the first `N` keys. -/
structure MassVector where
  /-- Mass carried by the `i`-th heaviest key. -/
  p : ℕ → ℚ
  /-- Number of keys carrying mass. -/
  N : ℕ
  nonneg : ∀ i, 0 ≤ p i
  sorted : Antitone p
  vanishing : ∀ i, N ≤ i → p i = 0
  total : ∑ i ∈ range N, p i = 1

namespace MassVector

variable (M : MassVector)

/-- Mass captured by the `k` heaviest keys. -/
def cumMass (k : ℕ) : ℚ := ∑ i ∈ range k, M.p i

lemma cumMass_mono : Monotone M.cumMass := by
  intro a b hab
  exact Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg (Finset.range_subset_range.mpr hab)
    (fun i _ _ => M.nonneg i)

lemma cumMass_N : M.cumMass M.N = 1 := M.total

lemma cumMass_le_one (k : ℕ) : M.cumMass k ≤ 1 := by
  rcases le_total k M.N with h | h
  · rw [← M.cumMass_N]; exact M.cumMass_mono h
  · refine le_of_eq ?_
    rw [← M.cumMass_N]
    refine (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.range_subset_range.mpr h) ?_).symm
    intro i _ hi
    exact M.vanishing i (by simpa using hi)

/-- The attention profile of a mass vector, carrying an arbitrary tokenizer
density `d` (the density is a free label: see `tpw_knee_decoupled`). -/
noncomputable def toProfile (d : ℚ) : AttentionProfile where
  tpw := d
  cum := M.cumMass
  cum_zero := by simp [cumMass]
  cum_mono := M.cumMass_mono
  cum_le_one := M.cumMass_le_one
  approaches_one := fun σ hσ => ⟨M.N, by rw [M.cumMass_N]; exact hσ.le⟩

@[simp] lemma toProfile_cum (d : ℚ) : (M.toProfile d).cum = M.cumMass := rfl

/-- The collision index `S = ∑ p i ^ 2`; `1 / S` is the effective number of
participating keys. -/
def collision : ℚ := ∑ i ∈ range M.N, M.p i ^ 2

lemma partial_collision_le (k : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ range k, M.p i ^ 2 ≤ M.collision := by
  rcases le_total k M.N with h | h
  · exact Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg (Finset.range_subset_range.mpr h)
      (fun i _ _ => sq_nonneg _)
  · refine le_of_eq ?_
    refine (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.range_subset_range.mpr h) ?_).symm
    intro i _ hi
    have : M.N ≤ i := by simpa using hi
    rw [M.vanishing i this]; ring

/-- Cauchy–Schwarz on the top-`k` block. -/
lemma cumMass_sq_le (k : ℕ) : (M.cumMass k) ^ 2 ≤ (k : ℚ) * M.collision := by
  have hcs := Finset.sum_mul_sq_le_sq_mul_sq (range k) M.p (fun _ => (1 : ℚ))
  have h1 : (M.cumMass k) ^ 2 ≤ (k : ℚ) * ∑ i ∈ range k, M.p i ^ 2 := by
    simpa [cumMass, mul_comm] using hcs
  have h2 : (k : ℚ) * ∑ i ∈ range k, M.p i ^ 2 ≤ (k : ℚ) * M.collision := by
    have : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (k : ℚ) := by positivity
    exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (M.partial_collision_le k) this
  linarith

/-- **Participation bound.**  The knee is at least `τ²` times the effective
number of participating keys `1 / S`.  This is a purely relational statistic of
the attention distribution: no property of the tokenizer enters. -/
theorem kneeAt_ge_sq_div_collision {d τ : ℚ} (hτ0 : 0 < τ) (hτ1 : τ < 1)
    (hS : 0 < M.collision) :
    τ ^ 2 / M.collision ≤ ((M.toProfile d).kneeAt τ : ℚ) := by
  set k := (M.toProfile d).kneeAt τ with hk
  have h1 : τ ≤ M.cumMass k := by
    have := (M.toProfile d).kneeAt_spec hτ1
    simpa using this
  have h2 : τ ^ 2 ≤ (M.cumMass k) ^ 2 := by nlinarith
  have h3 : (M.cumMass k) ^ 2 ≤ (k : ℚ) * M.collision := M.cumMass_sq_le k
  rw [div_le_iff₀ hS]
  linarith

/-- Since the mass vector is sorted, no key carries more than `p 0`. -/
lemma cumMass_le_top (k : ℕ) : M.cumMass k ≤ (k : ℚ) * M.p 0 := by
  have : ∑ i ∈ range k, M.p i ≤ ∑ _i ∈ range k, M.p 0 :=
    Finset.sum_le_sum fun i _ => M.sorted (Nat.zero_le i)
  simpa [cumMass, mul_comm] using this

/-- **Top-mass bound.**  A domain whose heaviest key already carries mass `p 0`
needs at least `τ / p 0` keys.  Domains differ in their knees exactly insofar as
they differ in this concentration statistic. -/
theorem kneeAt_ge_tol_div_top {d τ : ℚ} (hτ1 : τ < 1) (hp : 0 < M.p 0) :
    τ / M.p 0 ≤ ((M.toProfile d).kneeAt τ : ℚ) := by
  set k := (M.toProfile d).kneeAt τ with hk
  have h1 : τ ≤ M.cumMass k := by
    have := (M.toProfile d).kneeAt_spec hτ1
    simpa using this
  have h2 : M.cumMass k ≤ (k : ℚ) * M.p 0 := M.cumMass_le_top k
  rw [div_le_iff₀ hp]
  linarith

end MassVector

/-! ## 2. A worked domain: four equally weighted keys -/

/-- The domain whose attention is spread evenly over four keys. -/
noncomputable def quadUniform : MassVector where
  p := fun i => if i < 4 then 1/4 else 0
  N := 4
  nonneg := by
    intro i
    by_cases h : i < 4 <;> simp [h]
  sorted := by
    intro a b hab
    by_cases hb : b < 4
    · have ha : a < 4 := lt_of_le_of_lt hab hb
      simp [ha, hb]
    · simp only [hb, if_false]
      by_cases ha : a < 4 <;> simp [ha]
  vanishing := by intro i hi; simp [Nat.not_lt.mpr hi]
  total := by norm_num [Finset.sum_range_succ]

lemma quadUniform_collision : quadUniform.collision = 1/4 := by
  norm_num [MassVector.collision, quadUniform, Finset.sum_range_succ]

lemma quadUniform_cum_two : quadUniform.cumMass 2 = 1/2 := by
  norm_num [MassVector.cumMass, quadUniform, Finset.sum_range_succ]

lemma quadUniform_cum_three : quadUniform.cumMass 3 = 3/4 := by
  norm_num [MassVector.cumMass, quadUniform, Finset.sum_range_succ]

/-- The participation bound is attained on this domain: at tolerance `3/4` it
predicts `k* ≥ 9/4`, and the true knee is `3`. -/
theorem quadUniform_knee_three (d : ℚ) :
    (quadUniform.toProfile d).kneeAt (3/4) = 3 ∧
    (3 / 4 : ℚ) ^ 2 / quadUniform.collision ≤ 3 := by
  constructor
  · refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
    · refine (quadUniform.toProfile d).kneeAt_le ?_
      rw [MassVector.toProfile_cum, quadUniform_cum_three]
    · by_contra hlt

      have hle2 : (quadUniform.toProfile d).kneeAt (3/4) ≤ 2 := by omega
      have hspec := (quadUniform.toProfile d).kneeAt_spec (τ := 3/4) (by norm_num)
      have hmono := (quadUniform.toProfile d).cum_mono hle2
      rw [MassVector.toProfile_cum] at hspec hmono
      rw [quadUniform_cum_two] at hmono
      linarith
  · rw [quadUniform_collision]; norm_num

/-! ## 3. The exactly solvable decay family -/

/-- The geometric domain: the top-`k` keys capture `1 - r ^ k` of the mass, so
`r` is the decay rate of attention within the domain. -/
noncomputable def geometricProfile (d r : ℚ) (h0 : 0 < r) (h1 : r < 1) :
    AttentionProfile where
  tpw := d
  cum := fun k => 1 - r ^ k
  cum_zero := by simp
  cum_le_one := by
    intro k
    have : (0 : ℚ) < r ^ k := pow_pos h0 k
    show (1 : ℚ) - r ^ k ≤ 1
    linarith
  cum_mono := by
    intro a b hab
    have hp : r ^ b ≤ r ^ a := pow_le_pow_of_le_one h0.le h1.le hab
    show (1 : ℚ) - r ^ a ≤ 1 - r ^ b
    linarith
  approaches_one := by
    intro σ hσ
    obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := exists_pow_lt_of_lt_one (show (0 : ℚ) < 1 - σ by linarith) h1
    exact ⟨n, by linarith⟩

@[simp] lemma geometricProfile_cum (d r : ℚ) (h0 : 0 < r) (h1 : r < 1) (k : ℕ) :
    (geometricProfile d r h0 h1).cum k = 1 - r ^ k := rfl

/-- **Exact solution of the geometric domain.**  Keeping `k` keys suffices
exactly when the residual mass `r ^ k` has fallen below the slack `1 - τ`. -/
theorem kneeAt_geometric_le_iff {d r τ : ℚ} (h0 : 0 < r) (h1 : r < 1)
    (hτ1 : τ < 1) (k : ℕ) :
    (geometricProfile d r h0 h1).kneeAt τ ≤ k ↔ r ^ k ≤ 1 - τ := by
  constructor
  · intro hle
    have hspec := (geometricProfile d r h0 h1).kneeAt_spec hτ1
    have hmono := (geometricProfile d r h0 h1).cum_mono hle
    have : τ ≤ 1 - r ^ k := by
      simpa using le_trans hspec hmono
    linarith
  · intro hr
    exact (geometricProfile d r h0 h1).kneeAt_le (by simp; linarith)

/-- Slower decay never helps: the knee is monotone in the decay rate. -/
theorem kneeAt_geometric_mono {d r s τ : ℚ} (hr0 : 0 < r) (hr1 : r < 1)
    (hs0 : 0 < s) (hs1 : s < 1) (hrs : r ≤ s) (hτ1 : τ < 1) :
    (geometricProfile d r hr0 hr1).kneeAt τ ≤ (geometricProfile d s hs0 hs1).kneeAt τ := by
  refine AttentionProfile.kneeAt_mono_profile _ _ hτ1 ?_
  intro k
  have : r ^ k ≤ s ^ k := pow_le_pow_left₀ hr0.le hrs k
  simp only [geometricProfile_cum]
  linarith

/-- **The domain shift, reproduced inside the model.**  Two domains with the
*same* tokens-per-word `d` but decay rates `1/2` and `9/10` have knees `2` and
`14` at the same tolerance `3/4`: a sevenfold gap generated purely by attention
decay, mirroring code (`k* = 12`) versus French (`k* > 32`) at nearly equal
token density. -/

statistics as the controlling quantities.  This cycle asks: *how much* of a

  knee curve is a faithful order-isomorphic shadow of the majorization order on
  attention profiles — the "relational structure" NET-73 points at is exactly a
  majorization order.
* `Catalog.NET73.knee_curve_determines_capture` — the knee curve determines the
  capture curve: two domains with the same knees at all tolerances have the same
  attention concentration (though possibly wildly different tokenizers).
* `Catalog.NET73.kneeAt_mix_sandwich` — **mixtures interleave.**  A corpus that
  mixes two domains with weights `λ, 1-λ` has a knee between the two component
  knees: `min ≤ k*_mix(τ) ≤ max`.  Consequence

/-! ## 1. Two orders on domains -/

/-- `P` needs no more keys than `Q`, at every admissible tolerance. -/
def KneeDominates (P Q : AttentionProfile) : Prop :=
  ∀ τ : ℚ, 0 < τ → τ < 1 → P.kneeAt τ ≤ Q.kneeAt τ

/-- `P`'s attention is at least as concentrated as `Q`'s: its top-`k` keys
capture at least as much mass, for every `k`.  For mass vectors of equal total
this is exactly the majorization order. -/
def CaptureMajorizes (P Q : AttentionProfile) : Prop := ∀ k, Q.cum k ≤ P.cum k

/-- Majorization implies knee dominance (the easy direction). -/
theorem kneeDominates_of_majorizes {P Q : AttentionProfile}
    (h : CaptureMajorizes P Q) : KneeDominates P Q :=
  fun _ _ hτ1 => AttentionProfile.kneeAt_mono_profile Q P hτ1 h

/-- Knee dominance implies majorization: if `P` ever captured strictly less at
some `k`, a tolerance placed in the gap would make `P` need more keys. -/
theorem majorizes_of_kneeDominates {P Q : AttentionProfile}
    (h : KneeDominates P Q) : CaptureMajorizes P Q := by

Everything below is exact rational arithmetic (fractions.Fraction) wherever a
theorem asserts an exact value, so the printed numbers *are* the theorem
statements rather than floating-point approximations of them.

Contents
--------
1.  The measured domain table and its two refuting statistics

2.  The order-theoretic obstruction: discordant / concordant pair certificates

3.  Capture curves, the knee functional, and the three concentration bounds
      k* >= tau/m,   k* >= tau/p0,   k* >= tau^2/S.
4.  The decoupling theorem: identical token density, arbitrary knee.
5.  The exactly solvable geometric family and the 2-vs-14 domain shift.
6.  Majorization duality and the mixture sandwich, checked on samples.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction as F
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  The measured data
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Four uncensored domains, in the order (code, prose-de, math, prose-en).
DOMAINS: List[str] = ["code", "prose-de", "math", "prose-en"]
TPW: List[F] = [F(1950, 1000), F(1885, 1000), F(1214, 1000), F(1173, 1000)]
KNEE: List[F] = [F(12), F(20), F(16), F(16)]

# The censored fifth domain: French, tpw 1.246, knee > 32 at the original grid.
FRENCH_TPW: F = F(1246, 1000)
FRENCH_KNEE_LOWER_BOUND: int = 32


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Rank statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ascending_ranks_ordinal(x: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    """Ordinal ranks 1..n, ties broken by index order (smallest value = rank 1)."""
    order = sorted(range(len(x)), key=lambda i: (x[i], i))
    ranks: List[F] = [F(0)] * len(x)
    for position, i in enumerate(order):
        ranks[i] = F(position + 1)
    return ranks


def ascending_ranks_competition(x: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    """Competition rank: 1 + number of strictly smaller entries."""
    return [F(1 + sum(1 for v in x if v < xi)) for xi in x]


def ascending_ranks_midrank(x: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    """Tie-averaged (fractional) ranks."""
    out: List[F] = []
    for xi in x:
        smaller = sum(1 for v in x if v < xi)
        equal = sum(1 for v in x if v == xi)
        # average of ranks smaller+1 .. smaller+equal
        out.append(F(2 * smaller + equal + 1, 2))
    return out


def spearman(r: Sequence[F], s: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    """Spearman coefficient from the sum of squared rank differences."""
    n = len(r)
    d2 = sum((ri - si) ** 2 for ri, si in zip(r, s))
    return F(1) - F(6) * d2 / (F(n) * (F(n) ** 2 - 1))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Least-squares statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mean(x: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    return sum(x, F(0)) / F(len(x))


def cov(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    mx, my = mean(x), mean(y)
    return sum((xi - mx) * (yi - my) for xi, yi in zip(x, y))


def r_squared(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    return cov(x, y) ** 2 / (cov(x, x) * cov(y, y))


def least_squares_line(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> Tuple[F, F]:
    a = cov(x, y) / cov(x, x)
    b = mean(y) - a * mean(x)
    return a, b


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Order-theoretic certificates
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def discordant_pair(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> Tuple[int, int] | None:
    """A pair with x_i < x_j but not y_i < y_j: refutes every increasing law."""
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(x)), 2):
        for a, b in ((i, j), (j, i)):
            if x[a] < x[b] and not (y[a] < y[b]):
                return (a, b)
    return None


def concordant_pair(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> Tuple[int, int] | None:
    """A pair with x_i < x_j and y_i < y_j: refutes every decreasing law."""
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(x)), 2):
        for a, b in ((i, j), (j, i)):
            if x[a] < x[b] and y[a] < y[b]:
                return (a, b)
    return None


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Capture curves, knees, concentration statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def capture_curve(mass: Sequence[F]) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    """Prefix sums of a sorted-descending mass vector, saturating at the total."""
    prefix: List[F] = [F(0)]
    for m in mass:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + m)

    def C(k: int) -> F:
        return prefix[min(k, len(prefix) - 1)]

    return C


def knee(C: Callable[[int], F], tau: F, ceiling: int = 10_000) -> int:
    """Least k with C(k) >= tau."""
    for k in range(ceiling + 1):
        if C(k) >= tau:
            return k
    raise ValueError("tolerance not reached below the ceiling")


def collision_index(mass: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    """S = sum p_i^2; 1/S is the effective number of participating keys."""
    return sum((m * m for m in mass), F(0))


def concentration_bounds(mass: Sequence[F], tau: F) -> Dict[str, F]:
    """The three certified lower bounds on the knee."""
    sorted_mass = sorted(mass, reverse=True)
    p0 = sorted_mass[0]
    step_cap = p0  # for a sorted vector the largest single step is p0
    S = collision_index(sorted_mass)
    return {
        "per-key bound  tau/m": tau / step_cap,
        "top-mass bound tau/p0": tau / p0,
        "participation  tau^2/S": tau * tau / S,
    }


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Model families
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def uniform_profile_curve(tau: F, k: int) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    """Each of the first k keys carries tau/k: knee is exactly k at tolerance tau."""
    def C(j: int) -> F:
        return min(F(1), F(j) * tau / F(k))
    return C


def geometric_profile_curve(r: F) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    """C(k) = 1 - r^k: residual attention decays at rate r."""
    def C(k: int) -> F:
        return F(1) - r ** k
    return C


def geometric_knee(r: F, tau: F) -> int:
    """Least k with r^k <= 1 - tau (exact, by repeated multiplication)."""
    slack = F(1) - tau
    k, residual = 0, F(1)
    while residual > slack:
        residual *= r
        k += 1
    return k


def mixture_curve(lam: F,
                  CP: Callable[[int], F],
                  CQ: Callable[[int], F]) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    def C(k: int) -> F:
        return lam * CP(k) + (F(1) - lam) * CQ(k)
    return C


def majorizes(CP: Callable[[int], F], CQ: Callable[[int], F], upto: int) -> bool:
    return all(CQ(k) <= CP(k) for k in range(upto + 1))


def knee_dominates(CP: Callable[[int], F],
                   CQ: Callable[[int], F],
                   taus: Sequence[F]) -> bool:
    return all(knee(CP, t) <= knee(CQ, t) for t in taus)

    "demo_duality": """"
Randomised stress test of the structural theorems.

Three statements are checked on thousands of random attention profiles, in exact
rational arithmetic:

1. DUALITY.  P needs no more keys than Q at EVERY tolerance in (0,1) if and only
   if P's capture curve dominates Q's pointwise (majorization).  The easy
   direction is checked directly on a fine tolerance grid.  The hard direction is
   checked constructively: whenever majorization fails at some index k, the proof
   supplies the separating tolerance tau = (C_P(k) + C_Q(k)) / 2, and the test
   confirms that P's knee really is strictly larger there.

   The run also counts how often a *finite grid* of tolerances is fooled -- i.e.
   dominance appears to hold on the grid although majorization fails.  Those are
   exactly the cases where the separating tolerance falls between grid points,
   and they are why the theorem is stated over the continuum.

2. COMPLETENESS.  Two profiles with the same knee at every tolerance have the
   same capture curve.  Tested contrapositively: for every pair of distinct
   capture curves, an explicit tolerance is produced at which the knees differ.

3. MIXTURE SANDWICH.  The knee of a lambda-mixture always lies between the two
   component knees.

Run:  python3 demo_duality.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Sequence

random.seed(20260823)

NKEYS = 12
GRID: List[F] = [F(i, 40) for i in range(1, 40)]


def random_mass(n: int = NKEYS) -> List[F]:
    """A random probability vector on n keys, sorted heaviest first."""
    raw = [F(random.randint(1, 60)) for _ in range(n)]
    total = sum(raw, F(0))
    return sorted((w / total for w in raw), reverse=True)


def capture(mass: Sequence[F]) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    prefix: List[F] = [F(0)]
    for m in mass:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + m)

    def C(k: int) -> F:
        return prefix[min(k, len(prefix) - 1)]

    return C


def knee(C: Callable[[int], F], tau: F, ceiling: int = 4 * NKEYS) -> int:
    for k in range(ceiling + 1):
        if C(k) >= tau:
            return k
    raise ValueError("tolerance unreachable")


def majorizes(CP: Callable[[int], F], CQ: Callable[[int], F]) -> bool:
    return all(CQ(k) <= CP(k) for k in range(NKEYS + 1))


def dominates_on_grid(CP: Callable[[int], F], CQ: Callable[[int], F]) -> bool:
    return all(knee(CP, t) <= knee(CQ, t) for t in GRID)


def separating_tolerance(CP: Callable[[int], F],
                         CQ: Callable[[int], F]) -> Optional[F]:
    """The tolerance produced by the proof when majorization fails."""
    for k in range(NKEYS + 1):
        if CP(k) < CQ(k):
            tau = (CP(k) + CQ(k)) / 2
            if F(0) < tau < F(1):
                return tau
    return None


def mixture(lam: F, CP: Callable[[int], F], CQ: Callable[[int], F]
            ) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    return lambda k: lam * CP(k) + (F(1) - lam) * CQ(k)


def main(trials: int = 1200) -> None:
    easy_direction = 0        # majorization  =>  dominance on the grid
    witnesses = 0             # explicit separating tolerances verified
    grid_fooled = 0           # grid dominance despite failed majorization
    completeness = 0          # distinct capture curves separated by some knee
    sandwich = 0

    for _ in range(trials):
        CP, CQ = capture(random_mass()), capture(random_mass())
        maj = majorizes(CP, CQ)
        grid = dominates_on_grid(CP, CQ)

        # ---- 1. duality ----
        if maj:
            assert grid, "majorization failed to give knee dominance"
            easy_direction += 1
        else:
            tau = separating_tolerance(CP, CQ)
            if tau is not None:
                kP, kQ = knee(CP, tau), knee(CQ, tau)
                assert kP > kQ, "the proof's separating tolerance failed"
                witnesses += 1
                if grid:
                    grid_fooled += 1

        # ---- 2. completeness ----
        if any(CP(k) != CQ(k) for k in range(NKEYS + 1)):
            hi = CP if not maj else CQ
            lo = CQ if not maj else CP
            tau = separating_tolerance(lo, hi) or separating_tolerance(hi, lo)
            if tau is not None:
                assert knee(CP, tau) != knee(CQ, tau), "curves not separated"
                completeness += 1

        # ---- 3. mixture sandwich ----
        for lam in (F(0), F(1, 3), F(1, 2), F(4, 5), F(1)):
            CM = mixture(lam, CP, CQ)
            for tau in (F(1, 4), F(1, 2), F(3, 4), F(9, 10)):
                kp, kq, km = knee(CP, tau), knee(CQ, tau), knee(CM, tau)
                assert min(kp, kq) <= km <= max(kp, kq), "sandwich violated"
        sandwich += 1

    print(f"random profile pairs tested                : {trials}")
    print(f"majorization => knee dominance             : {easy_direction} ok")
    print(f"separating tolerance verified when it fails: {witnesses} ok")
    print(f"   (of these, a 39-point grid was fooled   : {grid_fooled})")
    print(f"distinct capture curves separated by a knee: {completeness} ok")
    print(f"mixture sandwich, 5 weights x 4 tolerances : {sandwich} ok")
    print("\nNo counterexample exists to find: all three are theorems.  The"
          "\n'grid fooled' count is the practical moral -- knee dominance must be"
          "\nchecked on the whole tolerance continuum, not on a sampled grid.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
",
    "algorithm_knee": """"
Algorithm A -- Knee extraction from a capture curve.

Given a nondecreasing capture curve C : N -> [0,1] with C(0) = 0, the knee at
tolerance tau is k*(tau) = min { k : C(k) >= tau }.  Monotonicity of C makes the
predicate "C(k) >= tau" upward closed, so bisection is correct: we first
exponentially expand a bracket until the predicate holds, then binary search
inside it.  Linear scan costs O(k*) curve evaluations; bisection costs
O(log k*) evaluations, which matters when each evaluation is a forward pass.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence


def knee_linear(C: Callable[[int], F], tau: F, ceiling: int = 100_000) -> int:
    """Least k with C(k) >= tau, by scanning.  O(k*) evaluations."""
    for k in range(ceiling + 1):
        if C(k) >= tau:
            return k
    raise ValueError("tolerance not attained below the ceiling")


def knee_bisect(C: Callable[[int], F], tau: F, ceiling: int = 1 << 30) -> int:
    """Least k with C(k) >= tau, by galloping then bisecting.  O(log k*)."""
    if C(0) >= tau:
        return 0
    hi = 1
    while hi <= ceiling and C(hi) < tau:
        hi *= 2
    if hi > ceiling:
        raise ValueError("tolerance not attained below the ceiling")
    lo = hi // 2                      # invariant: C(lo) < tau <= C(hi)
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if C(mid) >= tau:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid
    return hi


def knee_curve(C: Callable[[int], F], taus: Sequence[F]) -> List[int]:
    """The complete invariant: the knee at each tolerance in the list."""
    return [knee_bisect(C, t) for t in taus]


def capture_from_masses(mass: Sequence[F]) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    """Prefix-sum capture curve of a mass vector (sorted descending)."""
    prefix: List[F] = [F(0)]
    for m in sorted(mass, reverse=True):
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + m)

    def C(k: int) -> F:
        return prefix[min(k, len(prefix) - 1)]

    return C

    "algorithm_spearman": """"
Algorithm B -- Rank correlation under an explicitly declared tie convention.

Spearman's coefficient is 1 - 6*sum_i(r_i - s_i)^2 / (n(n^2-1)) for rank vectors
r, s.  Its value depends on how ties are broken, and the knee data contains a
tie (two domains at k* = 16).  This routine computes the coefficient under all
of the standard conventions at once, in exact rational arithmetic, so that a
reported number can never be an artifact of an undocumented choice:

    ordinal        ties broken by ascending index order (the reported choice)
    ordinal-alt    ties broken the other way round
    competition    1 + number of strictly smaller entries (ties share the low rank)
    midrank        ties receive the average of the ranks they span

On the measured data the four conventions give -2/5, -1/5, -1/10 and -1/4
respectively: the magnitude moves, the SIGN does not.  That robustness is the
reportable fact.  (A "dense" convention, which collapses tied values onto a
single rank with no gaps, is deliberately excluded: it discards the multiplicity
information that makes the coefficient comparable across vectors, and on this
data it returns exactly 0.)

Complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n^2) for the naive tie counts (O(n log n)
with a grouped scan).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence


def ranks_ordinal(v: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    order = sorted(range(len(v)), key=lambda i: (v[i], i))
    out: List[F] = [F(0)] * len(v)
    for position, i in enumerate(order):
        out[i] = F(position + 1)
    return out


def ranks_competition(v: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    return [F(1 + sum(1 for w in v if w < x)) for x in v]


def ranks_ordinal_alt(v: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    """Ordinal ranks with ties broken by descending index order."""
    order = sorted(range(len(v)), key=lambda i: (v[i], -i))
    out: List[F] = [F(0)] * len(v)
    for position, i in enumerate(order):
        out[i] = F(position + 1)
    return out


def ranks_midrank(v: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    out: List[F] = []
    for x in v:
        smaller = sum(1 for w in v if w < x)
        equal = sum(1 for w in v if w == x)
        out.append(F(2 * smaller + equal + 1, 2))
    return out


CONVENTIONS: Dict[str, Callable[[Sequence[F]], List[F]]] = {
    "ordinal": ranks_ordinal,
    "competition": ranks_competition,
    "ordinal-alt": ranks_ordinal_alt,
    "midrank": ranks_midrank,
}


def spearman_from_ranks(r: Sequence[F], s: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    n = len(r)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two observations")
    d2 = sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(r, s))
    return F(1) - F(6) * d2 / (F(n) * (F(n) ** 2 - 1))


def spearman_all_conventions(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> Dict[str, F]:
    """Exact Spearman coefficient of y on x under every tie convention."""
    return {name: spearman_from_ranks(rank(x), rank(y))
            for name, rank in CONVENTIONS.items()}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    tpw = [F(1950, 1000), F(1885, 1000), F(1214, 1000), F(1173, 1000)]
    knee = [F(12), F(20), F(16), F(16)]
    for name, rho in spearman_all_conventions(tpw, knee).items():
        print(f"{name:<13} rho = {str(rho):>6} = {float(rho):+.4f}")
    print("\nsign is negative under every convention -> "
          "the pre-registered rho >= 0.9 is refuted with the wrong sign.")

    "algorithm_certificate": """"
Algorithm C -- Monotone-law refutation certificates.

Given paired observables x (candidate explanation) and y (target), this routine
returns *proof objects* rather than p-values:

  * a discordant pair  (i, j)  with x_i < x_j and not y_i < y_j
    -- its existence refutes EVERY strictly increasing law y = f(x);
  * a concordant pair  (i, j)  with x_i < x_j and y_i < y_j
    -- its existence refutes EVERY strictly decreasing law y = f(x).

Correctness is the No-Monotone-Law Principle: a strictly increasing f preserves
strict order, so a discordant pair is a direct contradiction; a strictly
decreasing f reverses it, so a concordant pair is.  Naive scanning is O(n^2);
sorting by x and counting inversions in y reduces detection (though not witness
extraction with a prescribed shape) to O(n log n).

The routine also reports the two summary statistics for reference, so that the
weak (statistical) and strong (order-theoretic) refutations can be compared side
by side.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RefutationReport:
    discordant: Optional[Tuple[int, int]]
    concordant: Optional[Tuple[int, int]]
    spearman_ordinal: F
    r_squared: F

    @property
    def increasing_laws_refuted(self) -> bool:
        return self.discordant is not None

    @property
    def decreasing_laws_refuted(self) -> bool:
        return self.concordant is not None


def _ordinal_ranks(v: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    order = sorted(range(len(v)), key=lambda i: (v[i], i))
    ranks: List[F] = [F(0)] * len(v)
    for position, i in enumerate(order):
        ranks[i] = F(position + 1)
    return ranks


def _spearman(r: Sequence[F], s: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    n = len(r)
    d2 = sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(r, s))
    return F(1) - F(6) * d2 / (F(n) * (F(n) ** 2 - 1))


def _r_squared(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    n = len(x)
    mx = sum(x, F(0)) / F(n)
    my = sum(y, F(0)) / F(n)
    sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
    syy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y)
    if sxx == 0 or syy == 0:
        return F(0)
    return sxy * sxy / (sxx * syy)


def refute_monotone_laws(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> RefutationReport:
    """Search for both certificates and report both summary statistics."""
    n = len(x)
    discordant: Optional[Tuple[int, int]] = None
    concordant: Optional[Tuple[int, int]] = None
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            if i == j or not (x[i] < x[j]):
                continue
            if discordant is None and not (y[i] < y[j]):
                discordant = (i, j)
            if concordant is None and (y[i] < y[j]):
                concordant = (i, j)
    return RefutationReport(
        discordant=discordant,
        concordant=concordant,
        spearman_ordinal=_spearman(_ordinal_ranks(x), _ordinal_ranks(y)),
        r_squared=_r_squared(x, y),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    names = ["code", "prose-de", "math", "prose-en"]
    tpw = [F(1950, 1000), F(1885, 1000), F(1214, 1000), F(1173, 1000)]
    knee = [F(12), F(20), F(16), F(16)]

    rep = refute_monotone_laws(tpw, knee)
    print("Spearman (ordinal ranks):", rep.spearman_ordinal,
          f"= {float(rep.spearman_ordinal):+.3f}")
    print("R^2                     :", rep.r_squared,
          f"= {float(rep.r_squared):.6f}")
    if rep.discordant:
        i, j = rep.discordant
        print(f"increasing laws REFUTED by ({names[i]}, {names[j]}): "
              f"TPW {float(tpw[i]):.3f} < {float(tpw[j]):.3f} "
              f"but knee {int(knee[i])} >= {int(knee[j])}")
    if rep.concordant:
        i, j = rep.concordant
        print(f"decreasing laws REFUTED by ({names[i]}, {names[j]}): "
              f"TPW and knee both increase")

    "algorithm_concentration": """"
Algorithm D -- Concentration certificate for a cache budget.

Input: an empirical attention mass vector p (one entry per stored key, summing
to 1) and a tolerance tau in (0,1).

Output: the exact knee k*(tau) read off the prefix sums, together with three
CERTIFIED lower bounds that require no search:

    per-key bound        k* >= tau / m      where m = max_j (C(j+1) - C(j))
    top-mass bound       k* >= tau / p0     where p0 is the heaviest key
    participation bound  k* >= tau^2 / S    where S = sum_i p_i^2

The last is Cauchy-Schwarz on the top-k block, and 1/S is the effective number
of participating keys (inverse participation ratio, the exponential of the
Renyi-2 entropy).  All three are relational statistics of the attention pattern:
none of them refers to the tokenizer.

Complexity: O(n log n) dominated by the descending sort; the prefix sums,
p0 and S are each a single O(n) pass.  In deployment this turns a handful of
forward passes into a hard floor on the admissible cache size -- provisioning
below max(tau/p0, tau^2/S) keys is guaranteed to discard mass.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import List, Sequence


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ConcentrationCertificate:
    tolerance: F
    knee: int
    top_mass: F
    collision_index: F
    effective_keys: F
    bound_per_key: F
    bound_top_mass: F
    bound_participation: F

    @property
    def best_bound(self) -> F:
        return max(self.bound_per_key, self.bound_top_mass,
                   self.bound_participation)

    def is_sound(self) -> bool:
        return F(self.knee) >= self.best_bound


def concentration_certificate(mass: Sequence[F], tau: F
                              ) -> ConcentrationCertificate:
    if not (F(0) < tau < F(1)):
        raise ValueError("tolerance must lie strictly between 0 and 1")
    p: List[F] = sorted((m for m in mass), reverse=True)
    if not p or p[0] <= 0:
        raise ValueError("mass vector must have a positive heaviest key")

    prefix: List[F] = [F(0)]
    for m in p:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + m)

    knee = next((k for k in range(len(prefix)) if prefix[k] >= tau), None)
    if knee is None:
        raise ValueError("tolerance exceeds the total mass")

    p0 = p[0]
    step_cap = max(p)                      # largest single-key increment
    S = sum((m * m for m in p), F(0))

    return ConcentrationCertificate(
        tolerance=tau,
        knee=knee,
        top_mass=p0,
        collision_index=S,
        effective_keys=1 / S,
        bound_per_key=tau / step_cap,
        bound_top_mass=tau / p0,
        bound_participation=tau * tau / S,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    tau = F(3, 4)
    library = {
        "four equal keys": [F(1, 4)] * 4,
        "one dominant key": [F(4, 5), F(1, 10), F(1, 20), F(1, 20)],
        "geometric r = 9/10 (80 keys, renormalised)":
            [w / (F(1) - F(9, 10) ** 80)
             for w in (F(1, 10) * F(9, 10) ** i for i in range(80))],
    }
    for name, mass in library.items():
        cert = concentration_certificate(mass, tau)
        assert cert.is_sound()
        print(f"{name}:")
        print(f"   exact knee              {cert.knee}")
        print(f"   effective #keys 1/S     {float(cert.effective_keys):.3f}")
        print(f"   top-mass bound          {float(cert.bound_top_mass):.3f}")
        print(f"   participation bound     {float(cert.bound_participation):.3f}")
        print(f"   best certified floor    {float(cert.best_bound):.3f}\n")

def least_squares(x: List[float], y: List[float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return slope, intercept and coefficient of determination."""
    ax, ay = np.array(x), np.array(y)
    mx, my = ax.mean(), ay.mean()
    sxy = float(((ax - mx) * (ay - my)).sum())
    sxx = float(((ax - mx) ** 2).sum())
    syy = float(((ay - my) ** 2).sum())
    slope = sxy / sxx
    return slope, float(my - slope * mx), sxy * sxy / (sxx * syy)

    return ranks

    n = len(r)

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List, Sequence

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

TAU: float = 0.75


def geometric_capture(r: float) -> Callable[[int], float]:
    return lambda k: 1.0 - r ** k


def knee_of(C: Callable[[int], float], tau: float, ceiling: int = 400) -> int:
    for k in range(ceiling + 1):
        if C(k) >= tau - 1e-15:
            return k
    return ceiling


def capture_from_mass(mass: Sequence[float]) -> Callable[[int], float]:
    prefix = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(np.array(mass))])

    def C(k: int) -> float:
        return float(prefix[min(k, len(prefix) - 1)])

    return C


def tilted_mass(n: int, alpha: float) -> List[float]:
    """Mass vector p_i proportional to exp(-alpha * i), sorted descending."""
    w = np.exp(-alpha * np.arange(n))
    return list(w / w.sum())

    for a in alphas:

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

ADDITIONALLY — machine-readable directions block (REQUIRED). In
FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md, after the prose sections, emit a fenced JSON
array named future_directions.json with one object per direction
(3–6 entries), each with exactly these keys:
```json
[{"title": "<short noun-phrase name, NOT a sentence>",
  "domain": "<one of: NumberTheory, Algebra, Geometry, Combinatorics, Computation, Physics, Probability, Cryptography, Logic, MachineLearning, Tropical, Bridges>",
  "description": "<2-4 sentences: the conjecture, the approach, why it matters>",
  "conjecture": "<the precise mathematical claim>",
  "test": "<how to test or formalize it>",
  "if_true": "<consequence if true>",
  "if_false": "<consequence if false>",
  "proof_strategy": "<sketch of the proof route>",
  "catalog_references": ["<Catalog.lean.module>"]}]

Titles must be noun phrases ("Silver-Ratio Spectral Gap for Pell Spines"),
never sentences or recaps ("This cycle proved..." is forbidden).

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
            5. Build directly on existing catalog definitions — do not re-invent.

            ## Output Requirements
            Return ONLY:
            1. `.lean` files in `Catalog/Novelty/` with complete formal proofs.
            2. `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` with 3–5 concrete, falsifiable conjectures derived from your findings.
            3. `SELF_EVALUATION.json` with your honest self-assessment of the research:
               {
                 "quality_score": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "proof_depth": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "novelty": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "grade": "world_class" | "substantial" | "partial" | "shallow" | "trivial",
                 "rationale": "<2-3 sentence justification of grade and mathematical significance>"
               }

            Focus all compute budget on proving theorems.


### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce
computational evidence for the claim. Create a file named `ComputationalEvidence.md`
in the project directory with:

1. **Small-case calculations** — compute the first several instances of the object/conjecture.
2. **OEIS search results** — if a sequence appears, note its OEIS ID and first terms.
3. **Counterexample hunt** — test the universal claim on a representative sample; report any counterexample found.
4. **Plots or tables** — include any relevant visual/numerical data.

If you choose to skip this stage, you MUST explicitly justify why computational
evidence is unnecessary or infeasible in a `SkipEvidenceJustification.md` file.

Do not let the evidence stage dominate the project; keep it concise and directly
relevant to the theorem you intend to prove.

response, and showed that at bitlen 64 the 2-adic tie ceiling

zero-count statistic cannot explain the observed decline of the dial.

The natural next suspect is granularity of the **response**.  Here we prove the
two-sided law for *nested* profiles: if one variable's tie blocks refine the
other's, then

`ρ² = (V - T_coarse) / (V - T_fine)`,  where `V = (n³-n)/12`

/-- Sum of the fine midranks weighted by the fine block sizes, starting at offset `c`. -/
def wsum : List ℕ → ℚ → ℚ
  | [], _ => 0
  | p :: P, c => (p : ℚ) * (c + ((p : ℚ) + 1) / 2) + wsum P (c + p)

/-- The weighted mean of the fine midranks inside a coarse block is the coarse midrank. -/
lemma wsum_eq (P : List ℕ) (c : ℚ) : wsum P c = (P.sum : ℚ) * (c + ((P.sum : ℚ) + 1) / 2) := by
  induction P generalizing c with
  | nil => simp [wsum]
  | cons p P ih =>
      simp only [wsum, ih, List.sum_cons]
      push_cast
      ring

/-- Centred cross-product contributed by one coarse block with midrank `R`. -/
def spBlock (mu R : ℚ) : List ℕ → ℚ → ℚ
  | [], _ => 0
  | p :: P, c => (p : ℚ) * (R - mu) * ((c + ((p : ℚ) + 1) / 2) - mu) + spBlock mu R P (c + p)

lemma spBlock_eq (mu R : ℚ) (P : List ℕ) (c : ℚ) :
    spBlock mu R P c = (R - mu) * ((P.sum : ℚ) * ((c + ((P.sum : ℚ) + 1) / 2) - mu)) := by
  induction P generalizing c with
  | nil => simp [spBlock]
  | cons p P ih =>
      simp only [spBlock, ih, List.sum_cons]
      push_cast
      ring

/-! ## 2. Nested profiles -/

/-- Centred cross-product of the coarse midranks against the fine midranks. -/
def spNest (mu : ℚ) : List (List ℕ) → ℚ → ℚ
  | [], _ => 0
  | P :: L, c => spBlock mu (c + ((P.sum : ℚ) + 1) / 2) P c + spNest mu L (c + P.sum)

/-- **Nested midrank collapse.**  Even when the response is itself tied, as long as its blocks
refine the statistic's blocks, the centred cross-product equals the *coarse* between-block sum of
squares. -/
theorem spNest_eq_ssR_coarse (mu : ℚ) (L : List (List ℕ)) (c : ℚ) :

  induction L generalizing c with
  | nil => simp [spNest, ssR]
  | cons P L ih =>

/-- Superadditivity of `m ↦ m³ - m` on block splits. -/
lemma cube_sub_self_superadd (a b : ℚ) (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) :

  nlinarith [mul_nonneg ha hb, mul_nonneg (mul_nonneg ha hb) ha, mul_nonneg (mul_nonneg ha hb) hb]

/-- Splitting one block into parts can only decrease the tie correction. -/
lemma tieCorr_le_of_split (P : List ℕ) :
    tieCorr P ≤ ((P.sum : ℚ) ^ 3 - P.sum) / 12 := by
  induction P with
  | nil => simp [tieCorr]
  | cons p P ih =>

      have hP : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (P.sum : ℚ) := by positivity
      have hp : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (p : ℚ) := by positivity

      have hcast : (((p + P.sum : ℕ)) : ℚ) = (p : ℚ) + (P.sum : ℚ) := by push_cast; ring
      rw [hcast]
      linarith

theorem tieCorr_flatten_le (L : List (List ℕ)) :

      linarith

## Research context (FACT round-61 #1, exp 530, `U64-DIAL-HOLDS-COUNT-PARITY`)

The measurement under study reports a Spearman rank correlation between a
*zero-count statistic* `T` (the number of trailing binary zeros, i.e. the 2-adic
valuation, of a uniformly drawn integer) and a downstream `rate`, on uniform
draws at bitlen 64:

* seeds 20261140/41/42 give `0.658 / 0.642 / 0.643`;
* pooled `0.648`, CI `[0.629, 0.665]`, all inside the validation band `[0.55, 0.85]`;
* the dial declines gently from `≈ 0.78` at bitlen 44 to `≈ 0.65` at bitlen 64.

This file supplies the *mathematics* that such a dial needs: an exact,
closed-form ceiling for any Spearman coefficient measured between a tied
discrete statistic and any tie-refining response, together with the explicit
evaluation of that ceiling for the dyadic (2-adic valuation) tie profile of
uniform `b`-bit draws.

## Main results

* `sp_eq_ssR` — the *midrank collapse identity*: if the response ranking refines
  the blocks of the tied statistic, the centred cross-product equals the
  between-block sum of squares.  (Probabilistically: `Cov(R,S) = Var(R)` because
  `R = E[S | block]`.)
* `ssS_eq_ssR_add` — the *tie decomposition*: total centred sum of squares
  = between-block part + `Σⱼ (mⱼ³ - mⱼ)/12`.
* `spearmanSq_eq` — the **tie-attenuation law**

* `spearman_eq_one_iff` — `ρ = 1` exactly when there are no ties.
* `dyadic_spearmanSq` — for the 2-adic tie profile of uniform `b`-bit draws
  (`b ≥ 1`) the ceiling is **exactly** `ρ² = (6/7)·(1 + 1/(2^b(2^b+1)))`.
* `dyadic_ceiling_strict_anti`, `dyadic_ceiling_gt`, `dyadic_ceiling_tendsto` —
  the ceiling decreases strictly in the bitlen and converges to `6/7`
  (`ρ → √(6/7) ≈ 0.92582`) from above.
* `card_two_adic_block`, `dyadicBlocks_eq_valuation_profile` — the arithmetic
  bridge: the tie blocks of the trailing-zero statistic on `range (2^b)` have
  cardinalities `2^(b-1-k)` (plus the singleton `{0}`), which is exactly the

* `u64_inside_band`, `u64_below_tie_ceiling`, `tie_ceiling_insufficient`,
  `count_parity_gap` — the recorded round-61 numbers checked against the theory.

`tie_ceiling_insufficient` is the sharp negative result: between bitlen 44 and
bitlen 64 the tie-attenuation ceiling can drop by **less than `10⁻²⁶`**, while
the recorded dial drops by `0.78 → 0.648` (i.e. `≈ 0.188` in `ρ²`).  Hence the
observed monotone decline of the zero-fit dial is *not* a tie/quantisation
